For upgradeable contracts, the storage layout of different major versions should be assumed incompatible, for example, it is unsafe to upgrade from 4.9.3 to 5.0.0. Learn more at [Backwards Compatibility](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/backwards-compatibility). ## Overview ### Installation #### Hardhat (npm) ``` $ npm install @openzeppelin/contracts ``` #### Foundry (git) > [!WARNING] > When installing via git, it is a common error to use the `master` branch. This is a development branch that should be avoided in favor of tagged releases. The release process involves security measures that the `master` branch does not guarantee. > [!WARNING] > Foundry installs the latest version initially, but subsequent `forge update` commands will use the `master` branch. ``` $ forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts ``` Add `@openzeppelin/contracts/=lib/openzeppelin-contracts/contracts/` in `remappings.txt.` ### Usage Once installed, you can use the contracts in the library by importing them: ```solidity pragma solidity ^0.8.20; import {ERC721} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol"; contract MyCollectible is ERC721 { constructor() ERC721("MyCollectible", "MCO") { } } ``` _If you're new to smart contract development, head to [Developing Smart Contracts](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/learn/developing-smart-contracts) to learn about creating a new project and compiling your contracts._ To keep your system secure, you should **always** use the installed code as-is, and neither copy-paste it from online sources nor modify it yourself. The library is designed so that only the contracts and functions you use are deployed, so you don't need to worry about it needlessly increasing gas costs. ## Learn More The guides in the [documentation site](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts) will teach about different concepts, and how to use the related contracts that OpenZeppelin Contracts provides: * [Access Control](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/access-control): decide who can perform each of the actions on your system. * [Tokens](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/tokens): create tradeable assets or collectives, and distribute them via [Crowdsales](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/crowdsales). * [Utilities](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/utilities): generic useful tools including non-overflowing math, signature verification, and trustless paying systems. The [full API](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/api/token/ERC20) is also thoroughly documented, and serves as a great reference when developing your smart contract application. analysis.summary: Ownable is an abstract access-control module that designates a single owner and exposes an onlyOwner modifier for restricting functions. The owner can transfer ownership or renounce it; renouncing sets the owner to address(0), which permanently disables onlyOwner-gated functionality.

claims.statement: Ownable provides an onlyOwner modifier that restricts function calls to the current owner, reverting with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount for other callers.
renounceOwnership is callable only by the current owner and sets the owner to address(0) via _transferOwnership.
After renunciation, onlyOwner-gated functions can no longer be called, since no account can satisfy the owner check.
claims.quote:
NOTE: Renouncing ownership will leave the contract without an owner,
     * thereby disabling any functionality that is only available to the owner.

limitations: The excerpt covers only the Ownable module; privileged operations in inheriting contracts are not shown.
No security guarantees are implied; behavior depends on how inheriting contracts apply onlyOwner.

checks.scope: Schema and exact quotation checks only. Quotation presence does not establish semantic entailment.

analysis.summary: Pausable is an abstract module providing a paused-state flag, pause/unpause internal functions, and two modifiers that gate functions. It does not automatically pause anything; the inheriting contract must apply the modifiers and expose authorized pause controls.

claims.statement: Pausable supplies the whenNotPaused and whenPaused modifiers, which can be applied to functions of the inheriting contract.
claims.quote:
It will make available the
 * modifiers `whenNotPaused` and `whenPaused`, which can be applied to
 * the functions of your contract.

claims.statement: Including the module alone does not make functions pausable; the modifiers must be put in place by the integrating contract.
claims.quote:
Note that they will not be pausable by
 * simply including this module, only once the modifiers are put in place.

claims.statement: The pause and unpause entry points are internal and gated by modifiers, so the caller is responsible for exposing them with appropriate authorization.

limitations: The excerpt does not show any access-control mechanism (e.g., onlyOwner) on _pause/_unpause, so authorization requirements must be supplied by the inheriting contract.
No security guarantee is implied; the module only provides state and modifier logic as shown.

review.summary: All three draft entries are grounded in the supplied excerpts and correctly scoped. Ownable claims (onlyOwner reverting with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount, renounceOwnership setting owner to address(0), post-renunciation lockout) match source-1 and are properly labeled observation/inference. Pausable claims match source-2, including the explicit note that inclusion alone does not make functions pausable and that _pause/_unpause are internal with no access control shown. The evidence entry's README inference about master-branch installs lacking release-process security measures is directly supported by the quoted WARNING. Limitations appropriately flag the truncated README, absence of integrating application/deployment code, and that no security guarantee is asserted. No unsupported assurances, contradictions, or out-of-scope claims found.

issues.reason: Claim that onlyOwner reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount is not supported by the cited snippets; the error name appears only as a truncated doc comment ('The caller account is not authorized...') and no revert statement is shown. The specific error identifier is an invented detail beyond the excerpt.

Claim that _pause/_unpause are 'gated by modifiers' is only partially supported: the snippet shows _pause has whenNotPaused, but the _unpause modifier is cut off ('- The '). The inference that both entry points are modifier-gated and that caller must supply authorization is reasonable but the 'gated by modifiers' phrasing overstates what is visible for _unpause.

The README inference about 'dependency pinning and upgrade choices' goes beyond the snippet, which only warns against master-branch installs and notes forge update behavior. 'Upgrade choices' is not mentioned; this is an out-of-scope extrapolation.

priorReviews.summary: Draft is largely faithful and appropriately scoped, but three claims exceed the cited text: a specific revert error name not shown, a modifier-gating assertion for _unpause that is truncated, and a README inference about upgrade practices not present in the snippet. Recommend softening these to match visible evidence.
